time.desc: Leader A officially joined the short video platform Platform X and released its first video. The number of fans on the account exceeded 4 million within two days, far exceeding the opponent's campaign headquarters account, and the video views reached 69 million times. This marked a major change in his stance - during his tenure, he tried to ban Platform X through executive orders on the grounds of national security. Now he openly opposes the ban and warns that banning will only strengthen his competitors.
The short video platform confirmed that its private messaging function was used for zero-day vulnerability attacks and has taken measures to block and restore accounts.
The government submitted a defense document to the court, emphasizing that local isolation of data is not enough to eliminate national security threats and firmly defending the legality of the law

Institution B filed court documents detailing for the first time specific allegations that Platform X poses a national security threat, saying it provides City B with 'the means to undermine Country A's national security' by collecting vast amounts of sensitive data and using proprietary algorithms at Country B to control what users see, and that the algorithms can be manually manipulated to secretly shape the information Country A users receive; Platform X responded with a statement saying the government has never provided evidence for its accusations.
Federal appeals court filings defend "forced divestment or injunction" law and reveal central intelligence agencies' allegations about risks of data and content manipulation

The management of the national legislative body expanded the scope of the ban and required the removal of multiple applications owned by the short video platform’s parent company from the devices it manages.
The federal government and regulators filed a children's privacy-related civil lawsuit against the short video platform and its parent company
